name: Constitution of Georgia article 94 reform (Social-Democrats for the Development of Georgia and 25 organisations incl. GTUC, 2017)
detail: Appeal to delete the clause that bars higher taxes without a referendum, argued as opening the way to progressive taxation. About income tax rates; the report does not mention wealth.

name: Sopiko Japaridze, ConstitutionNet and Jacobin op-eds on article 94 (June 2017)
detail: Argue that article 94 forecloses "taxing the rich" and progressive taxation; no wealth tax is named and nobody is quoted in favour of one.

name: Georgian Trade Unions Confederation (GTUC) May Day manifesto (May 2023)
detail: The 2023 rally list expressly demands progressive income tax, not wealth tax. See https://netgazeti.ge/news/667543/?amp=1. This excludes the manifesto as evidence, not other potential GTUC statements.

name: Georgian property tax threshold change (2026) and income-threshold debate
detail: Annual property tax on specified assets and land; not a net-wealth tax. Revenue Service says the non-land income exemption threshold was raised from GEL 40,000 to 100,000 for 2026; see https://voice.rs.ge/Default.aspx?id=3874.

name: 2003 planned wealth tax (Zhvania government)
detail: 2003 proposal described taxes on expensive houses, holiday homes and cars; it is both pre-2010 and a specific-property tax, not demonstrated net-wealth taxation. See https://civil.ge/ka/archives/131239.

name: Georgian Dream offshore-assets tax amendments (April 2024) and critics
detail: The debate is about a tax exemption for repatriated offshore assets, criticised as serving Ivanishvili; no one calls for a wealth tax.

name: Tornike Chivadze, Arguments for a tax on the rich (2019)
detail: The essay argues for higher taxes on the rich and discusses income, land gains and inequality; it does not clearly propose a tax on the stock of net wealth.

name: Election Compass Georgia 2020 and 2024 rich-tax question
detail: The 2021 report lists all 30 2020 questions, including the question whether rich people should pay a larger share of income; the 2025 report likewise lists an income question. Neither is evidence of support for a net-wealth tax. The 2020 blog calls it wealth tax, but its grouped party summary is ambiguous.

name: Centre for Social Studies and authors: Striving for Shared Prosperity (2018)
detail: The recovered full text, especially reform agenda section 4.1, proposes three progressive personal income-tax scenarios and related spending. It does not establish support for a net-wealth tax. Publisher summary: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5402924

name: GTUC 2026–2029 action programme
detail: Calls for progressive taxation and below-subsistence wage income-tax relief; the programme does not state a wealth-tax base. Separately the 2023 rally explicitly demands progressive income tax.

name: Social Justice Center 2024 article on wealth filters
detail: Wealth filters are means tests for social-benefit eligibility; tax discussion concerns income-tax credits and relief, not a net-wealth tax.

name: FactCheck Georgia property tax fact-check (2025)
detail: The article uses the label wealth tax for the existing income-tested property tax on specified assets. Describing that tax does not advocate a net-wealth tax.

name: Transparency International Georgia tax-system overview (2010)
detail: Notes that Georgia lacks a wealth tax and progressive income-tax structure, but the cited discussion does not establish advocacy for a wealth tax.

name: Forbes Georgia, "How to tax progressively?" (July 2017)
detail: Argues that taxation in Georgia already works progressively through income and property tax; no wealth tax proposal.
